Oracle database found
 Potential 8

Explanation

Oracle database found. To migrate a Java application that uses an Oracle database to Azure, you can follow these recommendations:

* Migrate to Azure Database for PostgreSQL: Azure recommends migrating Oracle databases to Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server as it provides better cost-effectiveness and performance. Create a managed PostgreSQL Flexible Server database in Azure and choose the appropriate pricing tier based on your application's requirements.

* Use migration tools: Utilize the Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) or third-party tools to migrate your Oracle database schema and data to PostgreSQL. Consider using ora2pg or similar tools to convert Oracle-specific SQL to PostgreSQL-compatible SQL.

* Update database drivers and connection strings: Replace Oracle JDBC drivers with PostgreSQL drivers in your Java application. Update connection strings from Oracle format (jdbc:oracle:thin:) to PostgreSQL format (jdbc:postgresql:).

* Review and convert Oracle-specific code: Identify and convert Oracle-specific SQL functions, stored procedures, and PL/SQL code to PostgreSQL equivalents. Pay attention to data types, syntax differences, and built-in functions.

* Enable monitoring and diagnostics: Utilize Azure Monitor to gain insights into the performance and health of your Java application and the underlying PostgreSQL database. Set up metrics, alerts, and log analytics to proactively identify and resolve issues.

* Implement security measures: Apply security best practices to protect your Java application and the PostgreSQL database. This includes implementing authentication and authorization mechanisms with passwordless connections and leveraging Microsoft Defender for Cloud for threat detection and vulnerability assessments.

* Backup your data: Azure Database for PostgreSQL provides automated backups by default. You can configure the retention period for backups based on your requirements. You can also enable geo-redundant backups, if needed, to enhance data durability and availability.

Explanation

Using clear passwords in property files is a security risk, as they can be easily compromised if the files are accessed by unauthorized individuals. To enhance the security of your application, it is recommended to employ secure credential management practices.

* Azure Key Vault: Utilize Azure Key Vault to securely store and manage your application's passwords and other sensitive credentials. Azure Key Vault provides a centralized and highly secure location for storing secrets, keys, and certificates.

* Passwordless connections: You can provide an additional layer of security and convenience for accessing resources in Azure by eliminating the need for passwords. This way you can reduce the risk of password-related vulnerabilities, such as weak passwords or password theft.

Detects usage of Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs
 Potential 5
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 46

Explanation

The application depends on Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs (jakarta.persistence. or legacy javax.persistence.), which are used for object-relational mapping (ORM) and database interaction in Jakarta EE or Java EE applications.

When migrating to Azure:

  • Ensure that the database connection, JPA provider (e.g., Hibernate, EclipseLink), and dialect are compatible with your target Azure database service.
  • Recommended database services include Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Azure Database for MySQL, or Azure SQL Database.
  • For containerized deployments, these JPA-based applications can run on Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) or Azure App Service for Linux/Windows.
  • If using Spring Data JPA, verify that connection pool settings and environment variables are properly configured for the cloud environment.
  • Consider leveraging Azure Key Vault for secure storage of database credentials and connection strings.

CVE-2022-45868 — Password exposure in H2 Database

Severity: HIGH

Verified advisory identifiers: CVE-2022-45868; GHSA-22wj-vf5f-wrvj.

CVE reference: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2022-45868

Affected direct dependencies (Maven-resolved versions):

  • com.h2database:h2:2.1.214 (test; declared at pom.xml:89); validated affected range: >= 1.4.198, < 2.2.220.

Recommended fix:

  • Upgrade com.h2database:h2 to 2.2.220 or a later compatible release verified outside the affected range.

Applicability caveat: H2 is test-scoped, not a production runtime dependency. Exploitation requires starting the H2 web admin console with a cleartext -webAdminPassword CLI argument and local process-argument access. No such invocation or H2 console configuration was found in the repository. The vendor disputes the security classification, as documented in the advisory; this is a conditional test/tooling exposure, not a demonstrated production exploit.

Coverage: full-repository direct dependencies only (including test and optional dependencies); transitive packages are not advisory-scanned. Version presence is confirmed; exploitability is not proven. No tests or application builds were run.

Architecture Diagram

Photo Album is a single-module Java web application with server-rendered gallery pages, browser-side uploads, and Oracle-backed photo storage. This static assessment describes repository evidence, not a verified running deployment; credentials and secret values are omitted.

Data Storage & External Services

Oracle is the application's runtime datastore: the Photo entity maps to photos, including a photo_data LOB, filenames, MIME type, size, timestamp, and dimensions (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:15-90). Uploads read bytes into the database and image responses return those bytes through /photo/{id}; compatibility /uploads/ paths are not the active upload-storage mechanism (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:112-174, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:23-69). Compose persists Oracle files in oracle_data, mounts database initialization scripts, and waits for database health before starting the application (docker-compose.yml:12-22, docker-compose.yml:39-47).

The browser fetches Bootstrap assets from jsDelivr (src/main/resources/templates/index.html:7, src/main/resources/templates/index.html:124). No cache, message broker, outbound business API client, or object-storage integration was identified in the inspected application sources and runtime configurations. H2 is confined to tests. Database and administrator credentials are supplied through external configuration; values are not reproduced here (docker-compose.yml:30-36, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:34-42).

Key Architectural Decisions

  • Layered monolith with constructor injection: MVC controllers depend on the PhotoService interface; its implementation depends on PhotoRepository. The application is packaged as one JAR rather than independently deployed business services (pom.xml:15-18, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:24-32, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:28-48).
  • Database-centric binary storage with Oracle coupling: photo metadata and bytes share one entity, and native repository queries use ROWNUM, NVL, and TO_CHAR. Both runtime property files set Hibernate schema management to create, so schema recreation at startup is configured even though Compose retains database files (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:15-41, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:34-87, src/main/resources/application.properties:17-21, src/main/resources/application-docker.properties:13-17).
  • Synchronous secured mutations: upload and deletion execute within the HTTP request through transactional service methods. Security requires authentication for those POST routes, allows other requests, uses stateless HTTP Basic, and disables CSRF; the configured administrator is held in memory with a BCrypt-encoded password (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:28-61, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:28-30, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:54-55).

API & Service Communication Contracts

The application defines five HTTP controller operations: two HTML reads, one binary photo read, one multipart upload with JSON results, and one form-based deletion. Browser requests, controller-to-service calls, and persistence calls are synchronous; no asynchronous service messaging was identified.

Static assessment of repository source and deployment definitions only; no tests, deployment, or live endpoint verification were performed. References below are repository-relative paths with line numbers. No credential values are reproduced.

All paths are unversioned. No header/query version selector or application context-path override was identified.

ServiceMethodPathRequest TypeResponse Type

Explicit 400 JSON for an empty/null list reaching the handler; missing required part normally produces framework 400. Unauthenticated requests are challenged with HTTP Basic, normally 401.

photoalbum-java-app / PhotoFileControllerGET/photo/{id}String path parameter id; browser may append an unused _t cache-busting query200 ResponseEntity with ByteArrayResource image bytes and stored MIME type; 404 for absent photo/empty bytes; empty 500 response for caught exceptions.

Controller evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:37-98, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:18-78, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:23-86. Authentication evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:46-61.

Contract details:

  • Upload processing is sequential and is not an all-files atomic operation: each file calls the service independently. A successful upload is looked up again before inclusion in uploadedPhotos; if that lookup returns empty, no success or failure item is added for that file. That follow-up lookup is not caught by the controller, so an exception can escape rather than produce the documented per-file envelope (HomeController.java:68-97).
  • Service-level rejection is represented in failedUploads, not necessarily an HTTP 400. Multipart parsing can reject requests before controller execution; no custom multipart exception response contract was found. Validation details belong in business-workflows.md.
  • Image responses explicitly send Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate, private, Pragma: no-cache, Expires: 0, and X-Photo-ID, X-Photo-Name, X-Photo-Size headers (PhotoFileController.java:74-83).
  • Static CSS, JavaScript, and a bundled upload image are resources, not additional annotated controller operations. The returned filePath is a compatibility value, not the canonical retrieval endpoint; browser code constructs /photo/{id} (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:112-115,160-168; src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:176-179).

There are no gateway-level DTOs. The upload envelope has a boolean overall outcome and separate lists for successful and failed items; the explicit empty-input 400 instead contains success and error. Failure items contain the submitted filename and an error message (HomeController.java:58-65,85-95). See data-architecture.md for entity fields and persistence details rather than treating entities as a published schema.

The JSON starter supplies Jackson-based default conversion; no application-defined ObjectMapper, custom serializer, JSON naming strategy, OpenAPI/Swagger specification, protobuf schema, or GraphQL schema was identified. A LocalDateTime is inserted into upload-response metadata and consumed with JavaScript Date; there is no explicit application-level timestamp format/time-zone contract (pom.xml:75-79; HomeController.java:79; src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:161-170). HTML responses are template-rendered, and photo responses are raw bytes, not base64 JSON.

Communication Patterns

  • Browser and server: Same-origin HTTP form/navigation requests and fetch('/upload') with FormData. JavaScript's async/await is client-side request handling, not a message queue or asynchronous backend workflow (src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:90-132; src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:50,67,77-87).
  • Internal calls: Controllers invoke PhotoService directly; PhotoServiceImpl invokes PhotoRepository synchronously, with transactional service methods. Database communication uses JPA/JDBC, not another application's REST endpoint (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/PhotoService.java:13-54; PhotoServiceImpl.java:28-30,54-75,172-177,198-237; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:15-27).
  • Aggregation: No API gateway or multi-service response composition exists. Upload collects per-file outcomes locally, and the detail controller combines a photo with navigation identifiers from the same service (HomeController.java:68-95; DetailController.java:38-54). No gateway fallback is applicable.
  • Async/discovery/load balancing: No broker clients, event publishing, gRPC, Feign, REST/WebClient clients, service registry, or application-side load balancer were identified in the source/build. Compose resolves the configured database hostname on its bridge network; this is not registry-based application discovery (docker-compose.yml:31-34,49-51).
  • Resilience and timeouts: No explicit application retry policy, circuit breaker, bulkhead, fallback service, or request/query timeout value was found. Framework/driver defaults are not treated as verified timeout guarantees. Gallery errors fall back to empty HTML; detail errors redirect; binary serving errors return 500; upload service errors generally become failed results, while transaction completion and uncaught controller lookups may still propagate exceptions (HomeController.java:38-49,68-97; DetailController.java:38-58; PhotoFileController.java:84-86; PhotoServiceImpl.java:150-192). Container restart policy is not request retry.
  • API availability: Compose starts the application after database health succeeds; startup also requires externally supplied authentication/database credentials. Full readiness and startup configuration belong in configuration-inventory.md (docker-compose.yml:31-44; SecurityConfig.java:34-42).
  • Security contract: Stateless HTTP Basic authentication protects POST /upload and /detail/*/delete; all other requests are permitted. An in-memory user is assigned ADMIN, but the route rules require only authentication, not an explicit role check. CSRF is disabled; no JWT, OAuth2, method-level RBAC, or custom CORS policy was found (SecurityConfig.java:34-61). No application TLS connector, HTTPS enforcement, or TLS termination definition was identified in the inspected runtime configuration/Docker definitions; live ingress/transport security cannot be inferred. Clients should not assume Basic credentials are protected in transit.
  • Other external communication: Gallery HTML loads Bootstrap from an HTTPS CDN, a browser asset dependency rather than a backend business-service call (src/main/resources/templates/index.html:7). Azure provisioning uses control-plane commands and an external IP lookup; these are provisioning-time operations, not request-flow services (azure-setup.ps1:69-105,117-142,167).

Startup Dependency Chain

  1. Operator environment → Compose interpolation: ORACLE_PASSWORD, APP_USER_PASSWORD, and APP_ADMIN_PASSWORD must be supplied before Compose can resolve required expressions; credential usernames have masked fallbacks (docker-compose.yml:7-9,33-36).
  2. Oracle container → database initialization: Compose mounts oracle-init into the image initialization directory and persists database files in oracle_data (docker-compose.yml:12-14). 01-create-user.sql applies schema privileges, 02-verify-user.sql queries grants, and create-user.sh checks/creates the configured user (oracle-init/01-create-user.sql:14-33; 02-verify-user.sql:4-12; create-user.sh:24-41). Several SQL statements target a fixed credential identifier, whereas the shell uses APP_USER; arbitrary username overrides are not consistently propagated through the SQL files.
  3. Initialization shell → fixed delay: create-user.sh:15-17 waits 30 seconds before its SQL session; it does not implement a polling/retry loop. SQL runs against the Oracle pluggable database (create-user.sh:22).
  4. App container → healthy Oracle: Compose depends_on requires oracle-db to be service_healthy (docker-compose.yml:39-41). The actual configured readiness command is the image's healthcheck.sh, with 30-second interval, 10-second timeout, 15 retries, and 180-second start period (docker-compose.yml:17-22). The separate oracle-init/healthcheck.sql:1-3 is not the Compose healthcheck command.
  5. Application context → datasource and admin configuration: Spring uses the selected datasource settings and mandatory admin-password placeholder (application.properties:12-21; SecurityConfig.java:34-42). Compose applies restart: on-failure to the app (docker-compose.yml:44); no application readiness probe, explicit connection retry policy, or overall startup deadline is declared.
  6. Azure setup tooling → infrastructure sequence: Existing Azure CLI authentication is checked, then resource group → ACR → AKS → ACR attachment → PostgreSQL server/database/firewall rules → server FQDN → fixed 30-second delay → SQL role/grant setup → local environment-file output (azure-setup.ps1:45-197,206-299). This provisions infrastructure only; no checked-in deployment establishes a PostgreSQL-backed app readiness chain. No config-server/discovery-server startup dependency was found.

Secrets Provisioning Workflow

  • Local containers: Operator copies .env.example to ignored .env and supplies credentials; Compose interpolates names and injects Oracle credentials into the database and datasource/admin credentials into the app. Required password expressions fail early if unset/empty. Evidence: .env.example:1-17; .gitignore:201-204; docker-compose.yml:7-9,31-36. There is no checked-in encrypted store or explicit .env permission-hardening step.
  • Database access: The image receives application-user credentials; the mounted SQL scripts grant schema-scoped creation privileges, and the shell script authenticates administratively to create/check the configured application user. Evidence: oracle-init/01-create-user.sql:3-10,15-30; create-user.sh:11-35. Fixed SQL credential identifiers can diverge from overridden APP_USER; all identifiers remain masked here.
  • Application access: SecurityConfig.java:28-42,51-60 creates an in-memory admin identity, encodes the supplied password with BCrypt, and configures stateless HTTP Basic. BCrypt is password hashing in memory, not encryption of environment variables or deployment files.
  • Azure provisioning: An already authenticated Azure CLI session creates resources (azure-setup.ps1:45-58). PostgreSQL username/password variables are taken from the process or script fallbacks; missing passwords are generated with RandomNumberGenerator using a default length of 24 (:15-22,38-41). Administrative credentials are passed to Azure CLI/SQL operations, which create the application role and grants (:206-257). The application credentials are exported and written to the project-root .env (:274-299); no Kubernetes Secret creation or application binding is present.
  • Azure identity/access boundary: ACR is created with admin access enabled (azure-setup.ps1:69-74); AKS is attached to ACR (:102-105). No explicit database managed-identity/RBAC binding or Key Vault permissions are declared. The exact deployed identities/roles cannot be inferred from these commands alone.
  • Repository automation: Workflow secret references supply GitHub API/release automation; they do not provision Oracle/PostgreSQL credentials into a running application. The MCP example likewise has a separate developer-tool credential flow.

Core Business Workflows

Photo Album lets visitors browse a shared collection of uploaded images and navigate between individual photos. Authenticated users can add multiple photos and permanently remove photos from the collection.

Assessment is based on static inspection of src/main; runtime behavior was not tested. Source references below use repository-relative paths and line numbers. No credential values are reproduced.

Domain Entities

EntityService / Bounded ContextDescriptionKey Relationships
PhotoPhotoService / Photo collection managementAn uploaded image together with the descriptive information needed to display, navigate, and manage it. The only persisted business entity found; a standalone aggregate boundary is inferred, not an explicit DDD implementation.Contains the image content and its display metadata. Older and newer photos are computed navigation neighbors, not stored relationships. No album, owner, or user association is modeled.
UploadResultPhotoService / Upload processingTransient per-file outcome, not a persisted entity: communicates acceptance or rejection to the batch-upload coordinator.A successful outcome references a Photo; a failed outcome carries the submitted filename and explanation.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:12-19,28-108; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/UploadResult.java:3-29; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:220-237.

Service-to-Domain Mapping

This is one application with one business service, not independently deployed domain services. The following are in-process responsibilities within the same photo-management context.

ServiceDomain ContextOwned EntitiesExternal Dependencies
PhotoService / PhotoServiceImplUpload, retrieve, navigate, and delete collection itemsPhoto; produces UploadResultPhotoRepository and the photo database; image-header reader for optional dimensions
HomeControllerGallery presentation and batch-upload coordinationNone; composes Photo summaries and UploadResult outcomesPhotoService; browser upload interface
DetailControllerIndividual-photo viewing and removalNone; composes Photo and neighboring-photo identifiersPhotoService
PhotoFileControllerDelivery of stored image contentNone; reads Photo contentPhotoService

PhotoService is the business-operation boundary; the photo database is the durable source of truth for both metadata and image content. Controllers do not maintain independent copies. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:25-47,160-185,195-237; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:28-31,68-95; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:23-27,38-54; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:28-31,44-83.

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Upload multiple photos and publish them in the gallery

  1. A user selects or drops files into the gallery. The browser applies Client upload screening, then submits eligible files together to POST /upload. The authentication boundary requires an authenticated caller; the UI itself does not implement a login workflow.
  2. HomeController applies Batch presence, then iterates files sequentially. Each file is passed to PhotoService independently; there is no batch-level transaction.
  3. PhotoService applies Server upload eligibility and Image dimension ceiling. It reads the bytes, attempts optional dimension extraction, and creates a Photo using Photo identity and timestamp generation.
  4. The service saves the image content and metadata together, returning an UploadResult. Rejected files and caught read/save errors produce failure outcomes rather than intentionally undoing other files.
  5. For each reported success, HomeController looks the saved Photo up again and builds a display summary. It aggregates summaries and failures under Partial batch success.
  6. The browser shows successful and failed counts/messages, prepends accepted photos to the gallery, and requests their image content by identifier. Failed HTTP responses or network errors result in generic upload feedback; no automatic retry is implemented.

Evidence: src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:48-131,135-179; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:45-61; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:55-97; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:81-193.

Outcome caveat: the post-save lookup is outside the service upload error-handling block. A missing record is silently omitted from both result lists; a lookup exception can interrupt the request after earlier files have been saved. A successful batch response is therefore not guaranteed after every per-file save.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:68-95; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:67-75.

Workflow 2: Browse the collection and navigate individual photos

  1. A visitor opens GET /. HomeController retrieves the collection through PhotoService and PhotoRepository using Gallery chronological ordering, then renders image cards.
  2. The browser obtains each card's actual image from GET /photo/{id}. PhotoFileController retrieves the Photo, checks that content exists, and returns it with the stored media type. Image responses discourage reuse of stale content.
  3. Opening GET /detail/{id} retrieves the selected Photo, then separately retrieves its older and newer neighbors under Temporal navigation. The detail page combines metadata, image, and available navigation links.
  4. Read degradation determines the user experience on failure: gallery-load errors render an empty collection; invalid, missing, or failed detail loads redirect to the gallery; unavailable individual image content returns a not-found or server-error response rather than a replacement image.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:37-49; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:18-56; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:50-75,220-237; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:32-58; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:37-86; src/main/resources/templates/index.html:81-109; src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:62-94.

Workflow 3: Confirm deletion and remove a photo

  1. The detail page asks for browser confirmation before submitting POST /detail/{id}/delete. This is a presentation safeguard, not server-side approval.
  2. After authentication, DetailController calls PhotoService. Under Delete existence, the service looks up the Photo and either returns not-found or deletes the record containing its metadata and image content.
  3. The controller adds success, not-found, or generic failure feedback and redirects to the gallery, which displays flash messages. There is no soft-delete, restore, or compensating business action in the traced implementation.

Evidence: src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:50-59; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:54-60; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:195-217; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:64-78; src/main/resources/templates/index.html:37-46.

No scheduled, event-listener, message-handler, or startup business-state initialization entry points were found in src/main/java; the application entry point only starts the application. Repository month filtering, pagination, and statistics methods are not exposed by the inspected business service/controllers and are not treated as active user workflows. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/PhotoAlbumApplication.java:9-14; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:58-100; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:50-237.

Cross-Service Data Flows

There are no backend-to-backend domain-service calls, gateway aggregations, events, or circuit breakers in the inspected application. Composition is synchronous and local:

  • Upload composition: browser → HomeController → PhotoService → photo database; after saving, HomeController rereads each successful Photo by its returned identifier and combines display summaries with rejection details. Binary content is not included in that summary; the browser subsequently retrieves it using the same Photo identifier.
  • Detail composition: DetailController retrieves the selected Photo, then resolves older and newer photos by upload timestamp and exposes only their identifiers as navigation links. The browser fetches image content separately. There is no cross-context join.
  • Storage boundary: image bytes are stored with the Photo. The generated /uploads/ path is compatibility metadata, not a second file-store source of truth or a storage fallback.
  • Degradation: upload supports mixed acceptance/rejection; gallery failures look like an empty collection; detail failures redirect home; image failures return 404 or 500. There is no alternate provider or cached business-data fallback.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:37-48,68-97; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:38-57; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:44-86; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:112-177,220-237; src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:110-121,176-185.

Business Workflow Sequence

The primary upload-and-view workflow below shows actual rejection/degradation branches, not a hypothetical circuit breaker. The authenticated branch assumes the batch-presence rule passes.

sequenceDiagram actor User as "Photo contributor" participant UI as "Gallery browser" participant Auth as "Authentication boundary" participant Home as "Upload coordinator" participant Svc as "Photo service" participant Photo as "Photo aggregate" participant Store as "Photo repository and database" participant Files as "Image delivery" User->>UI: Select or drop photos UI->>UI: Apply client upload screening UI->>Auth: Submit eligible files alt Caller is not authenticated Auth-->>UI: Reject upload and require authentication else Caller is authenticated Auth->>Home: Process submitted batch loop Each submitted file Home->>Svc: Accept photo for publication Svc->>Svc: Check upload eligibility and dimension ceiling alt File rejected or read fails Svc-->>Home: File failure with explanation else File eligible Svc->>Photo: Assign identity and upload time with image content Svc->>Store: Persist photo alt Save succeeds and transaction completes Store-->>Svc: Saved photo Svc-->>Home: Success with photo identifier Home->>Svc: Resolve saved photo for display Svc->>Store: Retrieve photo Store-->>Svc: Photo Svc-->>Home: Display information else Save error caught within upload Svc-->>Home: File failure with explanation end end end Home-->>UI: Accepted photo summaries and failed files UI-->>User: Update gallery and show outcomes UI->>Files: Request accepted photo content Files->>Svc: Retrieve photo by identifier Svc->>Store: Load photo Store-->>Svc: Photo or unavailable Svc-->>Files: Photo or failure alt Photo and content available Files-->>UI: Image content else Missing content or retrieval error Files-->>UI: Not found or server error end end

Evidence: upload, authentication, and image-delivery sources cited in Workflows 1 and 2. Transaction-completion and post-save-lookup exceptions can escape the illustrated per-file failure handling, as described below.

Business Rules & Decision Logic

Validation and business decisions

RuleImplemented behaviorEvidence
Client upload screeningBrowser accepts JPEG, PNG, GIF, and WebP declarations and files no larger than 10 MiB; only eligible files are submitted. This is advisory, not the authority for server acceptance.src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:60-87
Batch presenceA null or empty bound file list produces a bad-request result. No explicit file-count enforcement is present in the controller/service despite a configured maximum of 10 files.src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:57-69; src/main/resources/application.properties:28-30
Server upload eligibilitySubmitted content type, lowercased, must be in the configured allowlist; size must be positive and no greater than the configured maximum. Defaults allow the four formats above and 10 MiB per file; multipart limits additionally cap each file at 10 MB and the request at 50 MB. A missing content type falls into generic upload error handling, not a dedicated validation outcome.src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:41-47,86-110,186-189; src/main/resources/application.properties:24-30
Image dimension ceilingWhere an image reader is available, header-derived width × height must not exceed 40,000,000 pixels. No-reader cases continue without dimensions; IOExceptions reject the file, while other dimension-extraction exceptions log a warning and continue. Successful decoding or correspondence between declared MIME type and actual bytes is not required by this path.src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:34-35,117-158
Photo metadata constraintsDeclared entity validation requires nonblank original/stored filenames up to 255 characters, nonblank MIME type up to 50 characters, a file path up to 500 characters, positive nonnull size, and a nonnull upload time. These are entity constraints, not a separate controller validation stage. Image content itself has no nonempty entity-validation annotation; content delivery checks it separately.src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:28-79; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:57-62
Photo identity and timestamp generationEach constructed Photo receives a new identity and current local upload time. A separate generated filename preserves the submitted extension as compatibility metadata. There is no content-deduplication or original-filename uniqueness check in this upload path.src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:93-108; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:112-115,160-177,243-248
Partial batch successEach file is processed separately. Overall success is true only when at least one saved Photo is successfully reread and added to the response. A processed batch returns HTTP 200 even if all files are rejected; an absent post-save record contributes neither a success summary nor a failure item.src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:68-97
Gallery chronological orderingPersisted gallery results are newest first. Newly uploaded cards are prepended; displayed size is derived from bytes and dimensions are shown only when available.src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:18-27; src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:154-158,172-196; src/main/resources/templates/index.html:104-107
Temporal navigationPrevious selects the first strictly older photo ordered newest first; next selects the first strictly newer photo ordered oldest first. Equal timestamps do not become neighbors, empty neighbor results hide the relevant link, and navigation does not wrap around.src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:29-56; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:220-237; src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:74-94
Delete existenceA missing Photo returns false; an existing Photo is deleted. There is no lifecycle status column or soft-delete business transition in the model/service.src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:195-217; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:19-108
Read degradationCollection-read failure renders an empty gallery; missing/invalid/failed detail retrieval redirects home. Image requests with invalid identifiers, missing photos, or absent bytes return 404; caught delivery errors return 500.src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:37-49; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:32-58; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:37-86

Lifecycle, integrity, and cross-cutting concerns

  • Lifecycle: submitted file → rejected outcome or persisted Photo → physically deleted record. There are no explicit approval, moderation, draft, recovery, or album-membership states. Metadata and image content are saved as one Photo; no bidirectional entity relationships require maintenance. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:81-193,195-217; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:19-108.
  • Transactions: PhotoServiceImpl has class-level transaction scope; retrieval and navigation methods are marked read-only. Each controller-to-service upload call has its own transaction boundary, not one transaction for the whole batch. Caught save errors do not guarantee a normal per-file outcome: transaction completion occurs outside the method body and can still fail. Detail composition spans separate service calls, not one controller-wide snapshot. No saga or compensation flow was found. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:28-30,53-75,173-193,223-237; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:68-91; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:38-52.
  • Error handling: upload uses UploadResult for expected rejections and caught processing failures; retrieval/deletion failures are wrapped in generic runtime exceptions. Controllers translate failures as described above; upload's post-save lookup has no equivalent catch. No domain-specific exception hierarchy, dead-letter path, or automatic retry appears in these flows. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/UploadResult.java:3-29; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:55-75,150-189,214-217; controller references above.
  • Audit/logging: upload rejection/success, deletion, retrieval errors, and image serving are logged. Image delivery also logs original filenames and a prefix of image bytes. These operational logs are not an attributable business audit trail: the Photo model does not record an authenticated uploader or deleter. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:91-102,179-189,203-216; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:45-72; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:19-108.
  • Authorization: gallery, detail, and image reads are public. Upload and delete require authentication through stateless HTTP Basic. One configured in-memory account is assigned ADMIN, but endpoint rules check authentication rather than the ADMIN role; no resource-ownership checks are modeled. Credentials are externally supplied and intentionally omitted here. The upload/delete controls remain visible in public templates; visibility does not grant permission. Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:34-61; src/main/resources/templates/index.html:48-77; src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:50-59; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:19-108.

Version & Compatibility Risks

The build targets Java 8 (pom.xml:23–26) and Spring Boot 2.7.18 (pom.xml:8–13), a legacy release line outside its original community support window. Moving to Spring Boot 3 or later requires a newer Java baseline (at least Java 17 for Boot 3) and review of the Jakarta namespace transition, particularly for JPA, validation, and web dependencies. Commons IO is explicitly pinned to the older 2.11.0 release (pom.xml:68–73); review maintained versions and advisories before modernization. Oracle and H2 compatibility cannot be established without resolving inherited versions. These are compatibility observations, not findings from a vulnerability scan.

Notable Observations

  • Most versions depend on one parent release; only Commons IO has an explicit dependency version (pom.xml:8–13, 30–101). Parent upgrades can therefore affect much of the dependency tree at once.
  • The explicit JSON starter is categorized as JSON support, despite the adjacent “Image processing” comment (pom.xml:75–79). Its potential overlap with the web starter should be checked against a resolved dependency tree, not assumed from source usage.
  • DevTools is optional but has default compile scope (pom.xml:95–100), so it remains in the non-test count. Optionality controls downstream propagation; it does not itself declare a test-only dependency.
  • Oracle is runtime-scoped while H2 is test-scoped (pom.xml:49–54, 88–93); the build declares different database dependencies for runtime and testing. Build files alone do not establish database behavioral parity.

No separate integration-testing, container-testing, or contract-testing library is explicitly declared. The local manifest does not establish test coverage or execution results, and no tests or dependency-resolution commands were run.

Data Architecture & Persistence Layer

The data layer contains one JPA entity, Photo, persisted through Spring Data JPA/Hibernate to Oracle, with H2 configured for the test profile. Photo bytes and metadata share the same relational table; there is no separate persisted album or user entity.

Evidence references below use repository-relative paths and source line numbers. This is a static source assessment, not verification of a running database; credential values are intentionally omitted.

UploadResult is an unannotated response object, not another persistent entity (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/UploadResult.java:1-14). Likewise, the administrator is represented in an in-memory security manager, not a JPA user model (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:33-42).

Transactions and storage: PhotoServiceImpl has class-level @Transactional; retrieval and older/newer lookup methods override this with read-only transactions (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:28-30,53-71,223-237). Upload reads the original file into a byte array and saves it with metadata; deletion removes the entity containing the LOB (PhotoServiceImpl.java:123-124,160-174,199-210). There is no separate object-store reference or active disk-write persistence path in that implementation.

photo-albumPhotoRepositoryList findAllOrderByUploadedAtDesc()Native SQL selecting all photo columns, including the LOB, newest first. Source: repository lines 22-27.

All six custom queries are declared with native @Query; timestamp, month, and pagination arguments use named parameter binding. No stored-procedure calls, named JPA queries, cross-service batch finders, or separate JDBC/MyBatis access layer were found.

The service calls the all-photos and older/newer custom queries; month, pagination, and statistics methods have no callers in the reviewed application source (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:53-75,223-237). Listing selects binary content as well as metadata, so it is not a lightweight metadata-only projection.

Data Ownership Boundaries

There is one application-owned relational data boundary: PhotoServiceImpl accesses PhotoRepository, which owns the Photo mapping and photos table. Within this application, readers and writers use the same entity and repository; there are no independent read/write stores, event projections, CQRS separation, or inter-service aggregation interfaces. Controller code delegates to PhotoService rather than accessing another service's database (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:28-40; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:23-26,39-49; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:28-32,45-58).

Default and docker configurations both describe Oracle storage; the test profile substitutes an in-memory H2 database. This is environment-level substitution, not evidence of database-per-service isolation. No second application service, shared-database consumer, cross-service REST data lookup, or message-based data replication was found in the reviewed source. External consumers and live database tenancy cannot be established from these files.

Metadata and original binary content have the same row lifetime and transactional ownership. Compatibility path/name fields do not establish another durable data store. There is no owner/user foreign key or row-level tenant mapping in Photo, so the entity model does not express per-user ownership (src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:15-108; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:112-124,160-174,199-210).
